title: Fine and gross motor

html:
Motor skills see noticeable refinement between ages 4 and 5, as children gain strength, balance, and dexterity. Gross motor abilities of a typical 4-year-old include running and jumping with confidence and the emerging ability to hop on one foot a few times in a row. By 4, most children can skip or gallop in an uneven rhythm and can navigate stairs one foot per step (alternating feet) when going down as well as up 1. They can also catch a large ball (though trapping it against the body is more common than a clean catch with hands at this age) and throw overhand with improved aim 1. Balance improves dramatically around this time: a four-year-old might manage to stand on one foot for about 4-5 seconds. By age 5, these gross motor skills become more advanced and integrated. Five-year-olds can typically balance on one foot for at least 5-10 seconds and walk heel-to-toe along a line 1. Many can skip with a smoother alternating gait and even attempt activities like jumping rope by the end of the fifth year 1. They also learn to hop forward on one foot and can walk backwards with balance 1. This improved coordination lets them start participating in group games and sports appropriate for preschoolers. Indeed, the transition to age 5 often corresponds with the ability to learn basic movement sequences (for example, a simple children’s dance or an obstacle course) and to adjust movements in response to obstacles or changes in terrain.

Fine motor skills also undergo important advances. At 4, children have sufficient fine motor control to draw basic shapes (circles, squares) and perhaps a very simple human figure (often a "tadpole" person with just a head and limbs). They can build tall block towers (8-10 blocks high) and are beginning to use child-safe scissors to snip paper 1. Four-year-olds can dress and undress with minimal help - for example, they can fasten large buttons and zip up a jacket if the zipper is started for them 1. By age 5, fine motor precision and hand-eye coordination have improved such that children can cut along a line with scissors and draw more recognizable objects. A five-year-old typically can draw a person with  6 body parts (head, body, arms, legs, etc.), whereas a 4-year-old’s drawing might only include 3 or 4 parts 1. Five-year-olds also master copying more complex geometric shapes: in addition to circles and squares, they can copy triangles and even basic diamonds by the end of this age 1. A study examines how children produce drawings (Figure) 2. The study shows annotated children’s drawings (Figure).

Age 5 is also when many children learn to write some letters and numbers. It’s common for 5-year-olds to be able to write their first name legibly and draw some letter forms (even if not perfectly formed) 1. They also often know how to hold a pencil with a proper tripod grasp, whereas a 4-year-old might still use a fisted or four-finger grasp for drawing. Five-year-olds enjoy crafts and construction play that challenge their fine motor skills: bead stringing, simple origami, small Lego assembly, etc., become easier and more enjoyable as their dexterity increases. By contrast, a 4-year-old can do puzzles and Duplo blocks, but a 5-year-old’s longer attention span and finer control often allow completion of more intricate puzzles (20+ pieces) and even basic Lego models.
